stem: Under RA 9745 (the Anti-Torture Act of 2009), in which case may a confession obtained as a result of torture be used as evidence?
choices: Against the person who confessed, if he signed it
Against the persons accused of doing the torture
In any case, as long as a lawyer was there too
In no case at all, in any proceeding whatsoever
answer: Against the persons accused of doing the torture
hints: The general rule in Section 8 of RA 9745 is strict, but it has one exception. Look for it.
Recall the rule: a confession, admission or statement obtained as a result of torture "shall be inadmissible in evidence in any proceedings".
Now read what follows the word "except". The exception helps punish the wrongdoers, not the victim. Find the choice that matches it.

solution.methodName: Find the rule, then check its exception

steps.action: Read the rule: "Any confession, admission or statement obtained as a result of torture shall be inadmissible in evidence in any proceedings".
steps.why: Inadmissible means the court cannot accept it as proof.

steps.action: Read the exception: "except if the same is used as evidence against a person or persons accused of committing torture."
steps.why: The statement can help prove that torture happened, so it may be used against the torturers.

steps.action: Signing it or having a lawyer present is not an exception in Section 8. And "in no case at all" ignores the exception.
The answer is: against the persons accused of doing the torture.

trapNotes.Against the person who confessed, if he: This is exactly what Section 8 forbids. A statement obtained through torture is inadmissible, signed or not.
trapNotes.In any case, as long as a lawyer was the: Section 8 has no lawyer exception. A statement obtained through torture stays inadmissible.
trapNotes.In no case at all, in any proceeding wha: Close, but Section 8 has one exception: the statement may be used as evidence against the persons accused of committing torture.
